# Complete Offline Build Manual — Low-Cost Greenhouse Air-Assisted Insecticide Sprayer

**Version 3 — prototype + large-scale greenhouse design**

This is a self-contained offline manual. It contains no web links and the configuration image is embedded inside this file.

The purpose of the machine is simple:

> **The nozzle makes the droplets small. The fan/blower carries those droplets through the vegetable canopy so less liquid falls directly to the floor.**

This manual focuses on the machine itself. It does **not** tell you to change pesticide concentration or label rates. When you eventually use a pesticide, the crop, greenhouse use, application method, PPE, ventilation, pre-harvest interval and re-entry interval must follow that product's label.

---

# 1. What to build first

Do **not** start by building a large greenhouse machine.

Build one small spray head first:

```text
TANK → PUMP → FILTER → GAUGE → REGULATOR → NOZZLE
                                               ↓
                                         FINE MIST
                                               ↓
                               BLOWER >>>>>>>>>>
                                               ↓
                                            PLANT
```

When one spray head works reliably, copy the same geometry into:

- left-side spray head
- right-side spray head
- multiple vertical nozzle zones
- moving cart or rail system

This modular approach is the easiest way to scale.

# 3. The most important technical idea

There are two separate jobs.

## Job A — atomization

This makes the droplets.

Main variables:

- nozzle design
- nozzle orifice
- pressure
- liquid flow
- liquid physical properties

## Job B — transport

This moves the droplets.

Main variables:

- fan/blower type
- air velocity
- air direction
- nozzle position relative to airflow
- nozzle distance from plant
- canopy density

A normal fan should **not** be expected to turn large droplets into small droplets.

If your current nozzle makes large drops, fix the nozzle/pressure side first.

---

# 4. Droplet-size target

For the type of greenhouse air-assisted mist system described here, a practical starting target is:

**50–100 microns**

For a simple DIY prototype:

**70–100 microns is a useful target zone.**

Do not try to create an ultra-fine room-filling fog.

Very tiny droplets can:

- remain airborne for too long
- evaporate faster
- move away from the crop
- increase inhalation exposure
- deposit unpredictably

Exact droplet size cannot be guaranteed just by looking at the spray. A real droplet-size measurement needs specialized equipment, so a DIY builder should use:

- a known agricultural nozzle
- stable pressure
- flow measurement
- water-sensitive cards
- floor-loss comparison

---

# 5. Prototype design target

A practical small prototype can use:

| Item | Starting design |
|---|---|
| Tank | 5–15 gal |
| Pump | 12 V diaphragm |
| Pump capability | roughly 40–70 PSI |
| Pump flow | roughly 1–2.2 GPM |
| Main liquid hose | about 3/8 in ID is a practical starting size |
| Nozzle branch hose | about 1/4 in ID is practical for short branches |
| Main strainer | around 50 mesh |
| Tip strainer | 50 or 100 mesh depending on nozzle |
| Gauge | 0–100 PSI |
| Nozzle type | fine hollow-cone |
| Nozzle material | ceramic preferred |
| Small blower | roughly 100–200 CFM per test head |
| Fan control | 12 V PWM speed control |
| Nozzle-to-near-leaf distance | start around 20–40 cm |
| Nozzle levels | 1 for testing, 2+ for real canopy |
| Power | 12 V battery or protected DC supply |

These are starting values, not pesticide-application instructions.

You need:

3. PWM speed controller
4. Short air duct or nozzle shroud
5. Blower mounting bracket
6. Adjustable air outlet
7. Optional simple plenum for several nozzles

You need:

1. 12 V power source

You need:

---

# 7. Nozzle — what to buy

For the first prototype, use a **small agricultural hollow-cone nozzle**.

Choose one with:

- published flow rating
- compatible pressure range
- replaceable tip
- matching tip strainer
- chemical-resistant body
- ceramic insert if affordable

Do not choose the nozzle only because the hole looks small.

The useful information is:

- flow at a known pressure
- spray angle
- droplet class or intended use
- recommended strainer mesh

---

# 8. Nozzle — what not to buy

Avoid these for the first prototype:

- air-induction nozzle
- flood nozzle
- large irrigation mist nozzle
- garden hose spray head
- unknown brass mist tip with no flow chart
- perfume atomizer
- humidifier disc
- homemade drilled hole

Air-induction agricultural tips are especially unsuitable when your current complaint is that the droplets are already too large.

---

# 9. How nozzle pressure affects your spray

In general:

```text
higher pressure
      ↓
more liquid velocity
      ↓
stronger breakup
      ↓
smaller average droplets
```

But there is a limit.

Too much pressure can cause:

- unnecessary airborne mist
- leaks
- faster wear
- pump overheating
- unstable operation

The correct approach is:

1. install the nozzle
2. use clean water
3. start at low/moderate pressure
4. increase gradually
5. measure nozzle flow
6. observe coverage
7. stop increasing when additional pressure no longer improves deposition

---

# 10. How to measure actual nozzle flow

You need:

- measuring jug
- stopwatch
- clean water

Procedure:

1. Set the machine to the selected pressure.
2. Put the nozzle into the measuring jug.
3. Spray for exactly 60 seconds.
4. Measure collected volume.
5. Repeat three times.
6. Average the readings.

Example:

```text
Run 1 = 0.16 gal
Run 2 = 0.15 gal
Run 3 = 0.16 gal

Average = 0.157 gal/min
```

Do this for every nozzle.

If one nozzle differs greatly from the others:

- clean it
- check its strainer
- replace it if necessary

---

# 11. Pump sizing formula

Your pump must supply every open nozzle at operating pressure.

Use:

```text
TOTAL NOZZLE FLOW = NUMBER OF OPEN NOZZLES × FLOW PER NOZZLE
```

Example:

```text
4 nozzles × 0.15 GPM = 0.60 GPM
```

Do not choose a 0.60 GPM pump for a 0.60 GPM requirement.

Leave headroom.

A practical design is to select a pump capable of at least roughly:

```text
1.5 × required nozzle flow
```

for a simple prototype, while also checking that it can provide the needed pressure.

Example:

```text
Required nozzle flow = 0.60 GPM

Minimum comfortable pump target:
0.60 × 1.5 = 0.90 GPM
```

A 1–2 GPM pump gives useful reserve.

---

# 12. Why pump flow and pressure are both important

A pump may advertise:

```text
2.0 GPM
70 PSI
```

That does **not** necessarily mean it delivers 2.0 GPM while simultaneously holding 70 PSI.

Pump flow usually falls as pressure rises.

Therefore:

- choose a pump with reserve
- check actual pressure while nozzles are open
- do not size only from the number printed on the pump

---

# 13. Tank construction

For the test unit:

- 5 gal is enough for bench testing
- 10 gal is comfortable
- 15 gal is good for a moving cart

The tank should have:

- large fill opening
- lid
- coarse fill screen
- bottom or low-side outlet
- drain
- vent
- secure mounting

Keep the tank low on the cart.

---

# 14. Tank outlet layout

Recommended:

```text
TANK
  ↓
FULL-PORT SHUTOFF VALVE
  ↓
COARSE SUCTION FILTER
  ↓
PUMP
```

The valve lets you:

- service the pump
- open the filter
- change a hose

without emptying the tank.

Use a full-bore valve so the suction line is not badly restricted.

---

# 15. Homemade coarse tank fill filter

This filter is easy to build safely because it is not pressurized.

Materials:

- plastic funnel or removable basket
- stainless or chemical-resistant nylon mesh
- plastic retaining ring
- simple handle

Construction:

```text
      LIQUID
        ↓
  ┌───────────┐
  │  FUNNEL   │
  │ ┌───────┐ │
  │ │ MESH  │ │
  │ └───────┘ │
  └─────┬─────┘
        ↓
       TANK
```

Make the mesh removable.

Do not glue it permanently.

Clean it every fill.

---

# 16. Homemade low-pressure suction filter

If you want to build a reusable filter yourself, the safest DIY place is on the **tank/suction side**, where pressure is low.

Use:

- large housing
- large screen area
- coarse mesh
- short suction hose

Do not make it too restrictive.

### Suggested construction concept

```text
TANK
  ↓
VALVE
  ↓
┌─────────────────────┐
│  LARGE FILTER BODY  │
│                     │
│  perforated tube    │
│  wrapped with mesh  │
│                     │
└──────────┬──────────┘
           ↓
          PUMP
```

Use a large-diameter housing so the filter does not starve the pump.

A blocked suction filter causes:

- pump cavitation
- rough noise
- pulsing
- low pressure

---

# 17. How to make the suction filter cartridge

Materials:

- perforated plastic support tube
- stainless or chemical-resistant nylon mesh
- two plastic end rings
- removable retaining clips

Construction:

1. Cut support tube to length.
2. Drill many smooth holes in the support tube.
3. Remove all drilling burrs.
4. Wash the tube.
5. Wrap mesh around the tube.
6. Overlap mesh slightly.
7. Secure the overlap without sharp metal edges.
8. Close one end.
9. Leave the outlet end open.
10. Slide cartridge into housing.

Flow concept:

```text
dirty liquid
    ↓
outside of mesh
    ↓
through mesh
    ↓
inside support tube
    ↓
pump inlet
```

---

# 18. Pressure-side filter

For the line after the pump, use a **basic pressure-rated agricultural inline strainer**.

Do not make this part from:

- drink bottle
- food jar
- thin transparent container
- non-pressure PVC container
- improvised glue-only housing

A pressure-side filter can fail violently if the housing is weak.

A simple commercial strainer is still a basic component, not advanced equipment.

Recommended layout:

```text
PUMP
  ↓
PRESSURE-RATED MAIN STRAINER
  ↓
GAUGE
  ↓
REGULATOR
  ↓
MANIFOLD
```

A roughly 50-mesh screen is a useful starting point for many fine-nozzle systems, but the nozzle's recommended mesh is the final guide.

---

# 19. Tip filters

Every nozzle should have its own small strainer.

Layout:

```text
MANIFOLD
   ↓
SMALL HOSE
   ↓
TIP STRAINER
   ↓
NOZZLE BODY
   ↓
NOZZLE TIP
```

This protects each tiny nozzle opening from particles that pass the main filter.

---

# 20. Filter maintenance

After every use:

1. stop pump
2. release pressure
3. close tank valve if needed
4. remove fill screen
5. clean suction filter
6. open main strainer
7. wash screen
8. remove tip filters
9. rinse them
10. inspect nozzle openings
11. flush clean water through hoses
12. reassemble

Do not allow pesticide residue to dry inside fine screens.

---

# 21. Pressure gauge installation

Install the gauge after the main strainer.

Good layout:

```text
PUMP → FILTER → GAUGE → REGULATOR → MANIFOLD
```

Why after the filter?

Because you want to know the pressure that is actually available to the nozzles.

Use a gauge that is easy to see.

A 0–100 PSI gauge is convenient for a 40–70 PSI prototype pump.

---

# 22. Regulator and bypass

A bypass regulator is useful.

It can send unused pump flow back to the tank.

```text
PUMP
  ↓
FILTER
  ↓
REGULATOR
  ├────→ NOZZLES
  │
  └────→ RETURN TO TANK
```

Advantages:

- stable pressure
- pump has somewhere to send extra flow
- return flow can provide gentle tank mixing
- easier adjustment

Avoid creating excessive foaming in the tank.

---

# 23. Optional pulsation damper

A small diaphragm pump can make pressure pulses.

Symptoms:

- gauge needle jumps
- cone pattern flickers
- hoses vibrate

Install a small accumulator after the pump/filter if needed.

```text
PUMP → FILTER → DAMPER → GAUGE → REGULATOR
```

This is optional at first.

---

# 24. Manifold construction

For a four-nozzle prototype:

```text
                ┌→ upper left
                ├→ lower left
MAIN LINE →─────┤
                ├→ upper right
                └→ lower right
```

Add a valve to each side:

```text
                LEFT VALVE → left nozzles
MAIN LINE → TEE
                RIGHT VALVE → right nozzles
```

This allows:

- left side only
- right side only
- both sides

---

# 25. Hose layout

A practical prototype layout is:

- larger hose from tank to pump
- medium main hose from pump to manifold
- smaller short branches to nozzles

Keep nozzle branch lengths similar when possible.

Why?

Very different branch lengths can produce different pressure losses.

Secure hoses so they cannot:

- touch wheels
- rub sharp edges
- kink
- hang into plants

---

# 26. Nozzle boom

Make a vertical boom on each side.

Cheap options:

- PVC pipe as structure only
- square aluminum tube
- light steel tube
- slotted metal channel

The boom does not need to carry liquid internally.

It can simply support:

- nozzle bodies
- hoses
- blower duct

This makes repairs easier.

---

# 27. Adjustable nozzle holders

Do not permanently glue a nozzle at one angle.

Use adjustable holders.

You need adjustment in:

- height
- vertical angle
- horizontal angle
- distance from fan outlet

Simple mounting methods:

- U-bolt
- hose clamp
- slotted bracket
- pivot bolt
- adjustable camera-style clamp

---

# 28. How many nozzle levels?

Use this rule for initial mechanical design:

```text
NUMBER OF LEVELS ≈ CANOPY HEIGHT / 30–50 cm
```

Round up.

Example:

```text
Canopy height = 120 cm
Spacing = 40 cm

120 / 40 = 3 nozzle levels
```

For a first test, use fewer.

For a large dense canopy, more individually controlled levels are better than one large nozzle.

---

# 29. Starting nozzle height arrangement

For a 1.2 m crop wall, an example test layout is:

```text
Nozzle 3: about 100 cm
Nozzle 2: about 60 cm
Nozzle 1: about 25–30 cm
```

These are only mechanical starting points.

Adjust according to:

- actual crop foliage
- pot/bed height
- lower canopy density
- aisle width

---

# 30. Nozzle angle

A useful starting configuration:

```text
upper nozzle: slightly downward + inward
middle nozzle: mostly inward
lower nozzle: slightly upward + inward
```

This encourages intersecting coverage.

Avoid aiming every nozzle exactly parallel.

---

# 31. Fan selection — prototype

A small directed blower is better than a normal wide open fan.

Useful types:

- inline blower
- centrifugal blower
- squirrel-cage blower
- compact EC/DC blower

For a small head, roughly **100–200 CFM** is a reasonable starting class.

CFM alone does not tell you how well it works.

The outlet size matters.

A small outlet can create a faster air jet than a large outlet at the same CFM.

---

# 32. Fan outlet and shroud

Do not simply point a naked fan toward the plant.

Build a short duct/shroud.

Example:

```text
BLOWER
  ↓
ROUND DUCT
  ↓
SHORT PLENUM
  ↓
NARROW OUTLET
  ↓
NOZZLE ZONE
  ↓
CROP
```

This makes the airflow:

- more uniform
- easier to aim
- less wasteful

---

# 33. Simple fan shroud construction

Low-cost materials:

- thin PVC sheet
- lightweight plastic board
- sheet aluminum
- round plastic duct

Make a short transition:

```text
round blower outlet
        ↓
 tapered transition
        ↓
 rectangular outlet
```

A rectangular outlet can cover several vertically spaced nozzles.

---

# 34. Air-plenum design for multiple nozzles

Instead of one fan per nozzle, one blower can feed several nozzles.

```text
       BLOWER
          ↓
     VERTICAL PLENUM
     ┌─────────────┐
     │ slot → N3   │
     │ slot → N2   │
     │ slot → N1   │
     └─────────────┘
          ↓
        CROP
```

This is much easier to scale.

Each slot directs air behind one nozzle level.

---

# 35. Best nozzle position relative to air

Place the nozzle near the air outlet.

A good concept:

```text
air outlet >>>>>>>>>>

             \ spray cone
              \ . . .
               \ . . .
                NOZZLE
```

The spray cone should enter the air stream quickly.

Do not place the nozzle so far downstream that large drops begin falling before the air reaches them.

---

# 36. Starting nozzle-to-blower spacing

Build the mount so the nozzle can move.

A useful mechanical test range is roughly:

**5–20 cm from the effective air outlet region**

Do not treat one distance as universal.

Test several positions.

The best position is the one that gives:

- even mist transport
- no wetting of the blower housing
- no severe spray distortion
- good canopy penetration

---

# 37. Starting nozzle-to-crop spacing

Start around:

**20–40 cm from the nearest leaf surface**

Then adjust.

Too far:

- mist spreads too much
- more floor loss
- more off-target deposition

Too close:

- local leaf soaking
- uneven coverage
- fan can damage or flatten leaves

---

# 38. How strong should the airflow be?

The best practical DIY indicator is the crop itself.

You want:

- visible gentle leaf movement
- inner leaves moving slightly
- no violent shaking

Too much air causes:

- spray passing through the crop
- wall deposition
- floor deposition
- plant damage
- unnecessary drift

For advanced testing, an inexpensive handheld air-speed meter is useful.

Measure air speed:

- at blower outlet
- halfway to crop
- at front canopy
- just behind canopy

The useful number is not only outlet speed; it is whether enough air reaches and penetrates the crop.

---

# 39. Fan speed control

Use a PWM controller compatible with the blower current.

Wiring:

```text
12 V SOURCE
   ↓
FUSE
   ↓
MASTER SWITCH
   ↓
PWM CONTROLLER
   ↓
BLOWER
```

Mark the controller:

```text
0
25%
50%
75%
100%
```

During testing, record the knob setting.

---

# 40. Pump electrical wiring

Recommended:

```text
12 V BATTERY
   ↓
MAIN FUSE
   ↓
MASTER DISCONNECT
   ├──── PUMP FUSE → PUMP SWITCH → PUMP
   │
   └──── FAN FUSE → PWM → BLOWER
```

Use separate branch fuses for pump and blower.

---

# 41. Large greenhouse electrical direction

For a large greenhouse, 12 V current becomes large over long wires.

A scalable design usually moves toward:

- 24 V DC equipment
- local fused controllers near each spray carriage
- protected power supply
- properly rated greenhouse wiring
- ground-fault protection where mains power is involved

Keep mains electricity and open electrical connections away from spray.

---

# 42. Prototype frame dimensions

You can adapt dimensions to your aisle.

A practical cart concept:

```text
width: aisle width minus at least 20–30 cm total clearance
length: 60–100 cm
tank mounted low
boom height: crop height + adjustment range
```

Example:

If aisle is 90 cm:

```text
cart width target ≈ 60–70 cm
```

This leaves room on both sides.

Do not build a cart that nearly touches the crop.

---

# 43. Cart layout

Side view:

```text
         upper nozzles
             |
         middle nozzles
             |
          blowers
             |
        ┌─────────┐
        │ controls│
        ├─────────┤
        │  tank   │
        ├─────────┤
        │ battery │
        │  pump   │
        └─────────┘
           wheels
```

Keep heavy components low.

---

# 44. Prototype assembly order

Build in this order.

## Stage 1 — frame

1. Measure aisle.
2. Build cart.
3. Mount tank.
4. Install vertical booms.
5. Check wheel clearance.
6. Push empty cart through greenhouse.

Do this before plumbing.

## Stage 2 — hydraulic system

7. Install tank valve.
8. Install suction filter.
9. Mount pump.
10. Install pressure filter.
11. Install gauge.
12. Install regulator.
13. Install manifold.
14. Run nozzle hoses.
15. Install tip strainers.
16. Install one test nozzle.

## Stage 3 — air system

17. Mount blower.
18. Install short duct/shroud.
19. Make blower angle adjustable.
20. Align blower with test nozzle.

## Stage 4 — electrical

21. Mount fused power box.
22. Connect master switch.
23. Wire pump.
24. Wire PWM controller.
25. Wire blower.
26. Secure all cables.

## Stage 5 — water test

27. Fill with clean water.
28. Leak-test at low pressure.
29. Increase pressure gradually.
30. Measure nozzle flow.
31. Test fan OFF.
32. Test fan ON.
33. Adjust nozzle/fan position.

Only after this should you add more nozzle levels.

---

# 45. Leak test

Use water only.

Procedure:

1. Fill tank halfway.
2. Open tank valve.
3. Check suction leaks before starting pump.
4. Start pump at low pressure.
5. Inspect every fitting.
6. Increase pressure gradually.
7. Hold operating pressure several minutes.
8. Check filter housings.
9. Check nozzle bodies.
10. Check regulator bypass.
11. Stop pump.
12. Check whether pressure falls quickly because of leaks.

Fix all leaks before continuing.

---

# 46. Suction-side air leak test

A suction air leak may not drip water.

Symptoms:

- pump sounds rough
- bubbles in clear line
- pressure oscillates
- spray pulses

Check:

- tank fitting
- valve
- suction filter lid
- hose clamp
- pump inlet threads

Use proper seals and clamps.

---

# 47. Water test — nozzle only

Fan OFF.

Record:

- pressure
- flow per minute
- spray cone appearance
- distance to plant
- floor collection

Do not change several things at once.

---

# 48. Water test — fan ON

Keep the same:

- pressure
- nozzle
- flow
- distance
- spray time

Turn fan on low.

Then test:

- low
- medium
- high

Observe:

- inner canopy movement
- floor wetness
- rear-side overspray
- leaf coverage

This directly shows whether air assistance is helping.

---

# 49. Water-sensitive paper layout

Place test cards:

```text
             TOP

front upper      rear upper

front middle     INNER     rear middle

front lower      lower inner

             FLOOR
```

If possible, put some cards under leaves.

You are trying to increase:

- inner canopy coverage
- underside coverage

while decreasing:

- floor coverage
- wall coverage

---

# 50. Simple floor-loss test

Place shallow trays or absorbent cards under a fixed test section.

Use the same spray time each run.

Compare:

```text
Run A: nozzle only
Run B: nozzle + low air
Run C: nozzle + medium air
Run D: nozzle + high air
```

The best fan setting is not necessarily the highest.

Choose the one that:

- improves plant deposition
- reduces floor loss
- does not push spray through the crop

---

# 51. Calibration notebook

For every test, record:

```text
Date:
Nozzle:
Pressure:
Nozzle flow:
Fan setting:
Nozzle height:
Nozzle angle:
Distance to crop:
Cart speed:
Plant height:
Plant density:
Floor wetness:
Inner coverage:
Outer coverage:
Comments:
```

This becomes your design data.

Without this record, it is easy to repeat the same mistakes.

---

# 52. Cart-speed calibration

If the cart is moving, speed changes application quantity.

Measure speed:

1. Mark a 10 m path.
2. Start normal walking/cart motion.
3. Time the travel.
4. Calculate:

```text
speed = distance / time
```

Example:

```text
10 m / 20 s = 0.5 m/s
```

Use the same speed during comparison tests.

---

# 53. Runtime calculation

If total nozzle flow is known:

```text
runtime = usable tank volume / total flow
```

Example:

```text
tank = 10 gal
total nozzle flow = 0.8 GPM

runtime = 10 / 0.8 = 12.5 minutes
```

Real runtime will be slightly lower because you should not depend on draining every last drop.

---

# 54. Large greenhouse — the wrong way to scale

Do not scale by simply installing:

- one huge fan
- one huge nozzle
- very high pressure

That usually creates:

- uneven coverage
- excessive drift
- giant wet zones
- poor inner-canopy control
- difficult maintenance

Scale by **repeating controlled modules**.

---

# 55. Large greenhouse — modular spray-head concept

A scalable system uses repeated zones.

Example:

```text
LEFT SIDE
Zone L1
Zone L2
Zone L3

CENTER CARRIAGE

RIGHT SIDE
Zone R1
Zone R2
Zone R3
```

Each zone can have:

- one nozzle
- one air slot
- optional solenoid valve

This makes the system easier to:

- tune
- repair
- automate
- turn off where there is no plant

---

# 56. Large greenhouse — central pump vs local pump

## Option A — pump on each cart

Advantages:

- simple
- independent
- short hoses

Disadvantages:

- many pumps to maintain
- many tanks to refill

## Option B — central tank + long hose

Advantages:

- one large tank
- one mixing station

Disadvantages:

- hose drag
- pressure drop
- difficult moving cart

## Option C — central supply + rail boom

Advantages:

- good for permanent large greenhouse
- organized movement
- fewer floor hoses

Disadvantages:

- more installation work

For a large permanent greenhouse, a moving rail/boom system is often more scalable than many independent small carts.

---

# 57. Large greenhouse — overhead rail idea

A simple large-scale concept:

```text
GREENHOUSE ROOF / SUPPORT
=========================
        RAIL
         |
      CARRIAGE
      /      \
 left head  right head
    ↓           ↓
  crop         crop
```

The carriage moves down the aisle.

Advantages:

- no floor obstacle
- repeatable path
- constant nozzle distance
- easier automation

---

# 58. Large greenhouse — existing irrigation boom reuse

If the greenhouse already has a moving watering boom, a future design can mount:

- spray manifold
- air ducts
- sensors

on the same moving structure, provided the structure is suitable and application rules allow it.

This reduces the need to build a separate robot.

---

# 59. Current trend — variable air assistance

One useful modern direction is:

> do not run the fan at one fixed maximum speed.

Instead:

- sparse plants → lower air
- dense plants → higher air
- empty gap → spray off

For a simple implementation, you do not need AI.

Use:

- 3 fan speed presets
- manual selection

Later, automate the fan speed.

---

# 60. Current trend — individually controlled nozzle zones

Instead of one valve controlling all nozzles:

```text
one solenoid per nozzle
```

or:

```text
one solenoid per vertical zone
```

Benefits:

- turn off upper nozzle when crop is short
- turn off a side with no plants
- reduce overspray
- easier troubleshooting

For a first large-scale version, zone control is more useful than expensive AI.

---

# 61. Current trend — PWM liquid control

A modern approach uses fast pulsing valves so flow can change without changing the basic nozzle pressure as much.

Concept:

```text
constant pressure
      ↓
PWM valve
      ↓
ON OFF ON OFF rapidly
      ↓
average flow changes
```

For your first prototype, use simple solenoid ON/OFF valves.

Add PWM later only after the hydraulic system works.

---

# 62. Current trend — variable-rate spraying

Instead of spraying the same amount everywhere:

```text
dense canopy → more flow
light canopy → less flow
empty space → OFF
```

A very simple version can use:

- distance sensor
- three flow levels

No camera is required at first.

---

# 63. Current trend — low-cost stereo or depth sensing

A scalable future machine can look at the crop and estimate:

- crop present/not present
- height
- width
- density

Then control:

- nozzle zones
- fan speed
- liquid flow

For the first version, use mechanical settings or simple distance sensors.

---

# 64. Current trend — sensor-guided plant detection

A simple sensor arrangement:

```text
upper sensor → checks upper canopy
middle sensor → checks middle canopy
lower sensor → checks lower canopy
```

Control example:

```text
no plant detected → nozzle OFF
plant detected → nozzle ON
dense plant → higher fan setting
```

This is a simple path to automation.

---

# 65. Current trend — air and liquid controlled separately

Modern systems increasingly treat air and liquid as separate controls.

That is important.

You should be able to adjust:

- liquid pressure/flow
- fan speed

independently.

Do not wire the system so the fan speed automatically changes every time pump speed changes.

---

# 66. Current trend — electrostatic assistance

Electrostatic charging can improve deposition on plant surfaces.

But for your project:

**do not add it to the first prototype.**

Reasons:

- high voltage
- humid greenhouse
- wet chemical spray
- more electrical design complexity

First prove:

- good nozzle atomization
- good airflow
- low floor loss

Then consider a professionally engineered electrostatic module.

---

# 67. Current trend — autonomous or rail-guided movement

Large greenhouses are moving toward repeatable machine travel:

- rail
- overhead carriage
- autonomous cart
- guided cart
- existing boom

The advantage is not just labor savings.

Repeatable movement gives:

- repeatable speed
- repeatable distance
- repeatable coverage

For a simple large-scale build, a guided rail can be easier than full autonomous navigation.

---

# 68. Current trend — data logging

Even a simple machine can record:

- pressure
- pump on/off
- fan setting
- cart speed
- total spray time
- tank volume used

You can later calculate:

- liquid used per aisle
- liquid used per plant area
- clogging frequency
- maintenance interval

A cheap controller can do this later.

---

# 69. Current trend — modular maintenance

Large machines are easier to maintain if each side is a replaceable module.

Example:

```text
LEFT SPRAY MODULE
- air duct
- 3 nozzles
- 3 strainers
- valve block

RIGHT SPRAY MODULE
- same parts
```

If one module fails, remove it and install a spare.

This is better than a machine where every hose and nozzle is permanently built into the frame.

---

# 70. Large-scale blower design

For a larger crop wall, instead of several tiny blowers, use:

- one efficient centrifugal blower per side
- vertical plenum
- several air slots

Example:

```text
        BLOWER
           ↓
     VERTICAL DUCT
    ┌─────────────┐
N4 ←│ air slot    │
N3 ←│ air slot    │
N2 ←│ air slot    │
N1 ←│ air slot    │
    └─────────────┘
           ↓
         CROP
```

This creates more consistent air from top to bottom.

---

# 71. Large-scale air balancing

If the top slot receives more air than the bottom slot, add simple adjustable shutters.

```text
slot 4 [adjustable opening]
slot 3 [adjustable opening]
slot 2 [adjustable opening]
slot 1 [adjustable opening]
```

Tune until canopy movement is similar at all heights.

---

# 72. Large-scale liquid manifold

Use separate branches:

```text
MAIN LIQUID LINE
       ↓
   ZONE BLOCK
   ├→ top
   ├→ upper-middle
   ├→ lower-middle
   └→ bottom
```

Add:

- shutoff valve or solenoid per branch
- serviceable strainer per nozzle
- labeled hoses

Do not use one long daisy-chain hose through every nozzle if you can avoid it.

---

# 73. Large-scale pressure monitoring

For a larger system, use:

- one main pressure gauge
- optional gauge at the end of long boom

If end pressure is much lower:

- hose too small
- filter blocked
- pump undersized
- flow too high

---

# 74. Large-scale pump sizing

Calculate:

```text
Q_total = sum of every nozzle flow that can be ON at once
```

Then add reserve.

Example:

```text
12 nozzles
0.12 GPM each

Q_total = 1.44 GPM
```

Choose a pump that can comfortably maintain the selected pressure above this flow.

For a large machine, do not use a tiny hobby pump near its limit.

---

# 75. Large-scale tank strategy

A large greenhouse can use:

## Small carriage tank

Good:
- easy plumbing
- no long hose

Bad:
- frequent refill

## Large central tank

Good:
- easier mixing
- fewer refills

Bad:
- long hose or central distribution system

## Hybrid

Central mixing station fills smaller carriage tanks.

This is simple and robust.

---

# 76. Large-scale cleaning station

Build a dedicated rinse/maintenance place.

Include:

- clean water
- drain/collection method allowed for the product
- soft brushes
- spare strainers
- spare nozzle tips
- O-rings
- gloves
- measuring jug
- tools

A large sprayer that is hard to clean will become unreliable quickly.

---

# 77. Large-scale automatic flush idea

A future version can have:

```text
spray tank valve
clean-water valve
        ↓
same pump
        ↓
lines/nozzles
```

After spraying, switch to clean water and flush.

Do not mix incompatible materials during cleaning.

---

# 78. Large-scale block detection

A blocked nozzle can be detected indirectly by:

- flow sensor
- pressure change
- camera
- operator inspection

The simplest method:

- inspect each spray cone during water test
- measure each nozzle flow regularly

A more advanced version adds a small flow sensor to each zone.

---

# 79. Large-scale spare strategy

Keep at least:

- 10% spare nozzle tips
- 10% spare tip strainers
- spare O-rings
- one spare solenoid per valve type
- one spare pressure gauge
- one spare blower controller
- spare fuses
- spare hose fittings

Standardize parts.

Do not use six different nozzle types on one machine unless there is a strong reason.

---

# 80. Prototype-to-large-scale roadmap

## Phase 1 — one head

Build:

- 1 nozzle
- 1 blower
- 1 filter chain
- 1 pump

Goal:

prove that air assistance reduces floor loss.

## Phase 2 — one side

Build:

- 2–3 nozzle levels
- one vertical air plenum
- one side of crop

Goal:

uniform top/middle/bottom coverage.

## Phase 3 — two sides

Duplicate the successful module.

Goal:

spray both sides of one aisle.

## Phase 4 — repeatable motion

Add:

- cart
- rail
- fixed travel speed

Goal:

repeatable application.

## Phase 5 — zone control

Add:

- solenoid valves
- left/right control
- vertical zones

Goal:

turn off unnecessary spray.

## Phase 6 — variable air

Add:

- electronic fan control
- preset or sensor-controlled fan speed

Goal:

match air to canopy density.

## Phase 7 — sensing

Add:

- distance sensors
- depth camera or stereo camera if needed

Goal:

automatically detect crop presence and size.

---

# 81. Recommended prototype configuration

A strong low-cost prototype would be:

```text
10–15 gal tank
   ↓
tank valve
   ↓
large coarse suction filter
   ↓
12 V 1–2.2 GPM diaphragm pump
   ↓
pressure-rated 50-mesh line strainer
   ↓
optional pulsation damper
   ↓
0–100 PSI gauge
   ↓
bypass regulator
   ├→ return to tank
   ↓
left/right manifold
   ├→ tip strainer → hollow-cone nozzle
   └→ tip strainer → hollow-cone nozzle

12 V blower
   ↓
PWM controller
   ↓
short duct/plenum
   ↓
air catches nozzle mist
   ↓
crop canopy
```

---

# 82. Recommended large-greenhouse module

Per side:

```text
1 centrifugal blower
1 vertical air plenum
3–5 adjustable air slots
3–5 nozzle levels
1 valve block
1 tip strainer per nozzle
1 detachable hose connection
```

Then mount:

```text
LEFT MODULE + CARRIAGE + RIGHT MODULE
```

This is much easier to scale than one huge nozzle/fan.

---

# 83. Troubleshooting table

| Problem | Most likely causes | First checks |
|---|---|---|
| Large droplets | wrong nozzle, low pressure, worn nozzle | nozzle type, gauge pressure |
| Spray pulses | pump pulsation, suction air leak | suction fittings, accumulator |
| One nozzle weak | clogged tip filter, nozzle clog | strainer, tip |
| All nozzles weak | blocked main filter, low pump voltage | main strainer, battery |
| Floor very wet | flow too high, drops coarse, weak air | nozzle, pressure, fan |
| Mist passes through crop | fan too strong | lower fan speed |
| Inner canopy dry | air too weak/wrong angle | fan position, air slot |
| Top wet/bottom dry | bad nozzle spacing | add/lower zone |
| Pump noisy | suction restriction/air | tank filter, hose |
| Pressure falls when all zones open | pump undersized or hose too small | calculate total flow |
| Fan gets wet | nozzle too close/wrong angle | reposition nozzle |
| Filter blocks quickly | dirty water/product solids/mesh too fine | fill screen, mesh selection |
| Nozzle flow keeps increasing | wear | compare against new tip |

---

# 84. Maintenance schedule

## After every use

- flush liquid system
- clean fill screen
- clean main strainer
- rinse tip strainers
- inspect nozzle spray
- wipe blower/shroud
- inspect leaks

## Weekly during frequent use

- measure nozzle flow
- check gauge
- inspect hoses
- inspect clamps
- inspect electrical connectors
- check fan bearings/noise

## Monthly

- compare nozzle flow with new nozzle
- inspect regulator
- inspect pump mounts
- inspect cart wheels
- inspect boom alignment
- check all fuses and switches

## Before storage

- completely clean system
- drain trapped liquid
- protect pump according to its instructions
- store nozzles clean
- disconnect power

---

# 85. What to measure before building the large version

Measure your greenhouse:

```text
Aisle width:
Crop height:
Crop wall thickness:
Row length:
Number of rows:
Distance between row centers:
Floor condition:
Available power:
Existing rail/boom:
Door width:
Maximum cart width:
```

These measurements determine the final frame.

---

# 86. How to calculate number of modules

For each crop side:

```text
vertical nozzle count ≈ canopy height / desired nozzle spacing
```

For total machine:

```text
total nozzles =
left levels + right levels
```

For several independent zones:

```text
total solenoids =
number of individually controlled zones
```

Keep the first large version simple.

Three vertical zones per side is often much easier to tune than ten independent nozzles.

---

# 87. Simple control logic for future automation

You can eventually implement:

```text
IF machine moving
AND plant detected
AND safety interlock OK
THEN
    pump ON
    required zone valves ON
    fan ON at selected level
ELSE
    spray valves OFF
```

Do not let the machine spray while stationary unless intentionally in a test mode.

---

# 88. Simple no-plant detection

A basic distance sensor can face the crop.

Example logic:

```text
distance < plant threshold
    plant present

distance > plant threshold
    empty gap
```

Then:

```text
empty gap → nozzle OFF
```

This can save liquid without AI.

---

# 89. Three-level canopy control

Simple version:

```text
Sparse canopy:
liquid zone ON
fan LOW

Medium canopy:
liquid zone ON
fan MEDIUM

Dense canopy:
liquid zone ON
fan HIGH
```

This is a practical interpretation of current variable-air trends.

---

# 90. Safety interlocks for large scale

A larger machine should include:

- emergency stop
- loss-of-motion spray shutdown
- low-tank sensor
- pump overcurrent protection
- fan guard
- pressure relief/bypass
- leak inspection
- door/area access procedure
- operator PPE procedure
- re-entry control

A useful rule:

```text
cart stops unexpectedly → spray valves close immediately
```

---

# 91. Why loss-of-motion shutdown matters

If a moving sprayer stops while spraying:

```text
same plant gets continuous spray
      ↓
over-wetting
      ↓
runoff
      ↓
floor waste
```

So a moving automated system should shut spray off when movement stops.

A wheel sensor or motor feedback can provide this later.

---

# 92. Do not use greenhouse circulation fans as your only spray fan

Normal greenhouse circulation fans are useful for general air mixing.

But they are not ideal for precise deposition because:

- airflow direction is broad
- distance varies
- neighboring rows are affected
- droplets can circulate around the room

Use local directed blower air at the spray head.

General greenhouse fans can be managed separately according to the application procedure.

---

# 93. Do not intentionally fill the whole greenhouse with fine aerosol

Your original goal is to keep droplets in the air longer.

The better engineering goal is:

> keep them airborne only long enough to reach and enter the crop canopy.

You want controlled transport, not indefinite suspension.

---

# 94. Final build checklist

Before first water run:

- [ ] tank secured
- [ ] tank valve installed
- [ ] fill screen installed
- [ ] suction filter clean
- [ ] pump securely mounted
- [ ] pressure filter installed
- [ ] gauge installed
- [ ] regulator/bypass installed
- [ ] hoses clamped
- [ ] nozzle tip installed
- [ ] tip strainer installed
- [ ] blower guarded
- [ ] blower bracket secure
- [ ] PWM controller fused
- [ ] master switch works
- [ ] wiring protected
- [ ] drain available
- [ ] water collection ready

---

# 95. First test checklist

- [ ] clean water only
- [ ] fan OFF
- [ ] low pressure
- [ ] check leaks
- [ ] raise pressure
- [ ] measure nozzle flow
- [ ] record spray pattern
- [ ] collect floor loss
- [ ] fan LOW
- [ ] repeat
- [ ] fan MEDIUM
- [ ] repeat
- [ ] fan HIGH
- [ ] repeat
- [ ] choose best deposition setting

---

# 96. Scaling checklist

Before making a large machine:

- [ ] one spray head proven
- [ ] nozzle model fixed
- [ ] operating pressure fixed
- [ ] filter mesh fixed
- [ ] fan type fixed
- [ ] nozzle/fan geometry fixed
- [ ] measured floor loss improved
- [ ] nozzle cleaning interval known
- [ ] measured pump flow sufficient
- [ ] left/right module tested
- [ ] travel speed defined
- [ ] safety shutdown planned

Only then duplicate the system.

---

# 97. Final recommendation

The most practical path for your idea is:

```text
FIRST:
fine hollow-cone nozzle
+ stable 40–70 PSI-class hydraulic system
+ good filtration
+ one controllable blower
+ water testing

THEN:
two or three nozzle levels
+ vertical air plenum
+ left/right modules
+ moving cart

THEN:
solenoid zones
+ variable fan speed
+ simple crop sensors

LATER:
rail movement
+ variable-rate control
+ camera/depth sensing
+ optional professionally engineered electrostatic assistance
```

This order keeps the project cheap at the beginning and makes every upgrade useful for the future large greenhouse system.

---

# 98. One-page component summary

## Prototype

```text
LIQUID:
10–15 gal tank
tank valve
coarse suction filter
12 V diaphragm pump
pressure-rated ~50-mesh strainer
0–100 PSI gauge
bypass regulator
manifold
tip strainers
ceramic hollow-cone nozzle(s)

AIR:
12 V directed blower
PWM controller
short duct/plenum
adjustable bracket

FRAME:
cart
left/right boom
adjustable nozzle clamps
low tank mounting

POWER:
battery/DC supply
master fuse
branch fuse
master switch
pump switch
fan PWM
protected wiring
```

## Large greenhouse

```text
one modular spray unit per aisle/carriage
3–5 vertical nozzle/air zones per crop side
centrifugal blower + vertical plenum per side
central or carriage pump sized for total flow
zone valves
repeatable travel path
movement interlock
eventual sensor-controlled variable air/flow
```

---

# 99. Final rule

If one small nozzle + fan module does not clearly improve plant coverage and reduce floor loss during water tests, **do not scale it yet**.

Fix the small module first.

Once the small module works, the large system becomes a repetition and control problem rather than a guessing problem.
